question: What is the primary skin layer targeted during an intradermal injection?
explanation: Intradermal injections are specifically delivered into the dermis, positioned directly underneath the outer epidermis. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T8#GNS125_U3_T8_h1)

question: Why is absorption significantly slower with intradermal injections?

options.A: Medications used are always oily suspensions
options.B: The needle depth blocks local circulation
options.C: The dermis has limited blood vessel supply
options.D: Skin cells in the dermis resist fluid

explanation: The relative lack of large blood vessels in the dermal layer causes medications to be absorbed gradually. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T8#GNS125_U3_T8_h1)

question: A Mantoux tuberculin skin test is administered via which route?
explanation: The Mantoux test requires precise intradermal placement to monitor local immune responses properly. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T8#GNS125_U3_T8_h2)

question: A patient requires routine screening for tuberculosis exposure. Which action should the nurse take?

options.A: Apply the testing solution topically over the chest
options.B: Administer the vaccine deep into the deltoid muscle
options.C: Inject the PPD antigen into the forearm dermis
options.D: Give the diagnostic dose through an intravenous line

explanation: Tuberculosis screening uses purified protein derivative delivered directly into the dermal layer of the forearm. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T8#GNS125_U3_T8_h2)

question: What is the maximum volume of medication typically given intradermally?
explanation: Intradermal doses are kept very small, usually not exceeding 0.1 mL, to prevent tearing the tight dermal tissue. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T8#GNS125_U3_T8_h3)

question: Which syringe type is standard for administering an intradermal injection?
explanation: Tuberculin syringes provide the fine measurement increments needed for tiny intradermal doses. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T8#GNS125_U3_T8_h3)

question: What is the preferred anatomical site for a standard tuberculin skin test?

options.B: Upper outer quadrant of the buttock

explanation: The forearm's inner surface provides easy access and clear visibility for reading skin test results. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T8#GNS125_U3_T8_h4)

question: Why should a nurse avoid scarred skin areas when choosing an injection site?

options.A: Blood vessels in scars increase bleeding risk
options.B: Scarred areas contain too many sensory nerves
options.C: Scar tissue alters absorption and obscures reactions
options.D: Fibrotic tissue causes needles to bend easily

explanation: Altered tissue integrity in scars can interfere with medication absorption and make skin reactions difficult to read. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T8#GNS125_U3_T8_h4)

question: At what angle should the nurse insert the needle for an intradermal injection?
explanation: A shallow angle of 5 to 15 degrees keeps the needle in the dermal layer just beneath the epidermis. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T8#GNS125_U3_T8_h5)

question: Why is massaging the injection site discouraged after an intradermal injection?

options.A: It destroys the needle tip inside the skin
options.B: It causes severe bruising and localized bleeding
options.C: It disperses medication into subcutaneous tissue

explanation: Rubbing or massaging the site forces the fluid away from the dermis, ruining the diagnostic test. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T8#GNS125_U3_T8_h5)

question: What part of a tuberculin skin reaction is measured to determine a positive result?
explanation: Only the hard, raised swelling (induration) is measured, ignoring simple surface redness. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T8#GNS125_U3_T8_h6)

question: A patient returns after 72 hours for a reading of their Mantoux test. What should the nurse assess?

options.A: Palpable hardness at the injection site
options.B: Elevation in the patient's body temperature
options.D: Fading of the initial injection blister

explanation: The 48-to-72-hour window is critical for assessing delayed hypersensitivity reactions manifested as induration. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T8#GNS125_U3_T8_h6)

question: What should the nurse do if no raised bleb appears during an intradermal injection?

options.A: Push more medication through the needle
options.B: Document the test as a negative result
options.C: Repeat the injection at a new site
options.D: Massage the area firmly to spread fluid

explanation: A missing bleb indicates the medication entered the subcutaneous tissue instead of the dermis, requiring a restart. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T8#GNS125_U3_T8_h7)

question: Which complication is most associated with allergy skin testing?
explanation: Itching at the test site is a frequent local reaction caused by histamine release during allergy evaluations. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T8#GNS125_U3_T8_h7)
